prompt: What is a Brønsted-Lowry acid?

choices.text: Any species that can donate a proton (H^+) to another molecule
Any species that can accept a proton from another molecule
choices.why: A proton acceptor is a Brønsted-Lowry base.

choices.text: Only a compound that increases the H^+ concentration in water
choices.why: That is the Arrhenius definition, which is limited to aqueous solutions. Brønsted-Lowry acids are proton donors in any reaction.

choices.text: Any species that contains an OH group
choices.why: Having OH doesn't make something an acid. A Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton.

explanation: A Brønsted-Lowry acid is any species that can donate a proton (H^+) to another molecule: a proton donor.

prompt: What is a Brønsted-Lowry base?

choices.text: Any species that can accept a proton from another molecule
Any species that can donate a proton to another molecule
choices.why: A proton donor is a Brønsted-Lowry acid.

choices.text: Only an ionic compound of the OH^− ion
choices.why: That describes classic Arrhenius bases. Brønsted-Lowry bases include species like NH3 that contain no OH^−.

choices.text: Any species that dissolves in water
choices.why: Dissolving isn't enough. A Brønsted-Lowry base accepts a proton.

explanation: A Brønsted-Lowry base is any species that can accept a proton from another molecule: a proton acceptor.

prompt: What limitation of the Arrhenius definition does the Brønsted-Lowry definition overcome?

choices.text: The Arrhenius definition is limited to aqueous solutions and to the H^+ and OH^− ions.
The Arrhenius definition can't describe any acid that contains oxygen.
choices.why: Arrhenius acids like HNO3 and H2SO4 contain oxygen. The limitation is that the definition depends on water.

choices.text: The Arrhenius definition applies only to gases.
choices.why: It applies to aqueous solutions. The Brønsted-Lowry definition is independent of water.

choices.text: The Arrhenius definition says acids and bases don't react with each other.
choices.why: Arrhenius acids and bases do react, in neutralization. The limitation is that the definition requires water.

explanation: The Arrhenius definition is limited to aqueous solutions and to the relationship between H^+ and OH^−. The Brønsted-Lowry definition focuses on proton transfer, so it applies to other reactions and is independent of water.

prompt: In the reaction H^+(aq) + OH^−(aq) → H2O(ℓ), how are H^+ and OH^− classified?

choices.text: H^+ is an acid and OH^− is a base by both the Arrhenius and the Brønsted-Lowry definitions.
H^+ is an acid only by the Arrhenius definition.
choices.why: H^+ is, by definition, a proton donor, so it is also a Brønsted-Lowry acid.

choices.text: OH^− is a base only by the Arrhenius definition.
choices.why: OH^− accepts the proton, so it is also a Brønsted-Lowry base.

choices.text: OH^− is the acid, because it reacts first.
choices.why: OH^− accepts the proton, which makes it the base.

explanation: The Brønsted-Lowry definition covers the Arrhenius one. H^+ is the proton donor and OH^− is the proton acceptor, so H^+ is an acid and OH^− is a base by both definitions.

prompt: Ammonia, NH3, has no OH^− in its formula. Why is it a base?

choices.text: It accepts a proton from H2O, forming NH4^+ and OH^− ions.
It donates a proton to H2O, forming NH2^− and H3O^+.
choices.why: Donating a proton would make NH3 an acid. With water, NH3 accepts a proton.

choices.text: It contains hidden OH^− ions in its structure.
choices.why: NH3 contains no OH^−. It makes OH^− by taking a proton from water.

choices.text: Any compound containing nitrogen is a base.
choices.why: Nitric acid, HNO3, contains nitrogen and is an acid. NH3 is a base because it accepts a proton.

explanation: NH3 generates OH^− ions in a proton-transfer reaction with water: NH3 + H2O → NH4^+ + OH^−. NH3 is the Brønsted-Lowry base (proton acceptor), and H2O is the acid (proton donor).

prompt: What is a hydrolysis reaction?

choices.text: A reaction with water
A reaction that produces hydrogen gas
choices.why: Hydrolysis means a reaction with water, such as NH3 hydrolyzing to NH4^+ and OH^−.

choices.text: The decomposition of water by electricity
choices.why: That is electrolysis. Hydrolysis is any reaction with water.

choices.text: A reaction that removes water from a compound
choices.why: Hydrolysis is a reaction with water, not a removal of it.

explanation: A reaction with water is called hydrolysis; for example, NH3 hydrolyzes to make NH4^+ ions and OH^− ions.

prompt: When HCl(g) dissolves in water, HCl(g) + H2O(ℓ) → H3O^+(aq) + Cl^−(aq). What role does H2O play?

choices.text: Brønsted-Lowry base: it accepts a proton from HCl.
Brønsted-Lowry acid: it donates a proton to HCl.
choices.why: H2O gains a proton here, becoming H3O^+, so it is the proton acceptor.

choices.text: Neither; water is only a solvent.
choices.why: Water takes part in the reaction, accepting HCl's proton.

choices.text: Both an acid and a base in this same reaction.
choices.why: Water can play either role, but in this reaction it only accepts a proton.

explanation: HCl donates a proton, so it is the Brønsted-Lowry acid. H2O accepts that proton to become H3O^+, so here it is the Brønsted-Lowry base.

prompt: What does it mean for a substance to be amphiprotic?

choices.text: It can act as either a proton donor or a proton acceptor.
It can't take part in proton transfer.
choices.why: It's the opposite: an amphiprotic substance can give or take protons.

choices.text: It is both an Arrhenius acid and an Arrhenius base at the same time.
choices.why: Amphiprotic refers to proton transfer: acting as a proton donor in one reaction and an acceptor in another.

choices.text: It contains two protons.
choices.why: The name is about behavior, not the number of protons: it can donate or accept one.

explanation: A substance that can act as a proton donor or a proton acceptor is called amphiprotic. Water is the most common example.

prompt: Water acts as a Brønsted-Lowry acid in its reaction with NH3 but as a Brønsted-Lowry base in its reaction with HCl. What does this show?

choices.text: Water is amphiprotic: its role depends on what it reacts with.
One of the two equations must be wrong.
choices.why: Both are correct. Water donates a proton to NH3 and accepts one from HCl.

choices.text: Water is always an acid and only appears to be a base.
choices.why: Water truly accepts a proton from HCl, becoming H3O^+; in that reaction it is a base.

choices.text: Water changes into a different substance before each reaction.
choices.why: It's the same H2O in both reactions; it simply donates or accepts a proton depending on its partner.

explanation: H2O can act as both a proton donor and a proton acceptor, depending on the other substance in the reaction. A substance that can do both is amphiprotic.

prompt: In the reaction HF + NH3 → NH4^+ + F^−, which species is the Brønsted-Lowry acid?

choices.text: HF
NH3
choices.why: NH3 gains a proton to become NH4^+, so it is the base.

choices.text: NH4^+
choices.why: NH4^+ is a product. On the reactant side, HF is the species that loses a proton.
F^− is what remains of HF after it donates its proton.

explanation: HF loses an H^+ to become F^−, so it is the proton donor, the Brønsted-Lowry acid. NH3 accepts the H^+ to become NH4^+, so it is the base.

prompt: In the reaction HNO2 + H2O → H3O^+ + NO2^−, which species is the Brønsted-Lowry base?

choices.text: H2O
HNO2
choices.why: HNO2 loses a proton to become NO2^−, so it is the acid.

choices.text: NO2^−
choices.why: NO2^− is a product. On the reactant side, H2O is the species that gains a proton.

choices.text: H3O^+
choices.why: H3O^+ is a product, formed when H2O accepts the proton.

explanation: H2O accepts an H^+ from HNO2 and becomes H3O^+, so H2O is the proton acceptor, the Brønsted-Lowry base.

prompt: In the reaction HSO4^− + OH^− → SO4^2− + H2O, which species is the Brønsted-Lowry acid?

choices.text: HSO4^−
OH^−
choices.why: OH^− gains a proton to become H2O, so it is the base.

choices.text: Neither, because an ion can't be an acid
choices.why: Ions can donate protons. HSO4^− gives up its H^+ to become SO4^2−.
SO4^2− is what remains after HSO4^− donates its proton.

explanation: HSO4^− donates a proton to OH^−, becoming SO4^2−, so it is the Brønsted-Lowry acid. Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases can be ions as well as molecules.

prompt: The reaction between NH3 and H2O does not go to completion. What happens instead?

choices.text: The reverse reaction also occurs, and eventually the two cancel out any further change: a dynamic equilibrium.
The reaction stops halfway, and all molecular activity ceases.
choices.why: At equilibrium both reactions are still occurring; they just balance each other. It is dynamic, not static.

choices.text: The NH3 slowly decomposes into N2 and H2.
choices.why: No decomposition is involved. The products react to re-form NH3 and H2O as fast as they form.

choices.text: The reaction keeps going until all the water is used up.
choices.why: It doesn't go to completion; the reverse process balances the forward one.

explanation: The reverse process occurs as well, and eventually the two processes cancel out any additional change. Both still occur, so the equilibrium is dynamic, and it is written with a double arrow: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4^+ + OH^−.

prompt: For NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4^+ + OH^−, consider the reverse reaction, NH4^+ + OH^− → NH3 + H2O. Which species is the Brønsted-Lowry acid in the reverse reaction?

choices.text: NH4^+
OH^−
choices.why: OH^− accepts a proton to become H2O, so it is the base in the reverse reaction.

choices.text: NH3
choices.why: NH3 is a product of the reverse reaction. NH4^+ donates the proton to form it.

choices.text: None; the reverse reaction isn't an acid-base reaction.
choices.why: The reverse reaction is also a proton transfer, so it is a Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reaction too.

explanation: In the reverse reaction, NH4^+ donates a proton to OH^−, so NH4^+ is the Brønsted-Lowry acid and OH^− is the base. Both directions are acid-base reactions.

prompt: What is a conjugate acid-base pair?

choices.text: Two species whose formulas differ by one proton, one acting as an acid and the other as a base
The acid and the base on the reactant side of an equation
choices.why: Those two belong to different pairs. Each pair links a reactant with the product it becomes after gaining or losing a proton.

choices.text: Any acid and any base that react with each other
choices.why: A conjugate pair is two forms of the same species, differing by one H^+.

choices.text: Two species that differ by an OH^− ion
choices.why: Conjugate pairs differ by a proton, H^+.

explanation: Within each conjugate pair, the two species differ by a proton in their formulas: the one with the extra proton is the conjugate acid, and the one without it is the conjugate base.

prompt: What is the conjugate base of HF?

choices.text: H2F^+
choices.why: H2F^+ has one more proton than HF; it would be HF's conjugate acid.

choices.text: OH^−
choices.why: A conjugate base comes from removing one proton from the acid itself: HF − H^+ = F^−.
H^+ is the proton that is removed. The conjugate base is what remains: F^−.

explanation: The conjugate base is the species left after the acid donates one proton: HF → F^−.

prompt: What is the conjugate acid of NH3?

choices.text: NH4^+
NH2^−
choices.why: NH2^− has one proton fewer than NH3; it is NH3's conjugate base.

choices.text: NH3^+
choices.why: Adding a proton (H^+) adds an H atom as well as a positive charge: NH4^+.

choices.text: OH^−
choices.why: OH^− is the conjugate base of H2O in the reaction of NH3 with water.

explanation: The conjugate acid has one more proton than the base: NH3 + H^+ → NH4^+. In NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4^+ + OH^−, NH4^+ is the conjugate acid of NH3.

prompt: What is the conjugate base of H2O?

choices.text: OH^−
H3O^+
choices.why: H3O^+ has one more proton than H2O; it is water's conjugate acid.
O^2− is two protons away from H2O. A conjugate base differs by just one proton.

choices.text: H2
choices.why: Removing a proton (H^+) from H2O leaves OH^−.

explanation: Removing one proton from H2O leaves OH^−, its conjugate base. Adding one gives H3O^+, its conjugate acid.

prompt: What is the conjugate acid of H2O?

choices.text: H3O^+
OH^−
choices.why: OH^− has one proton fewer than H2O; it is water's conjugate base.

choices.text: H2O2
choices.why: H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, a different compound. Adding a proton to H2O gives H3O^+.
H^+ is the proton added. The conjugate acid is H2O plus that proton: H3O^+.

explanation: Adding one proton to H2O gives H3O^+, its conjugate acid.

prompt: Which pair is a conjugate acid-base pair?

choices.text: HCO3^− and CO3^2−
H2SO4 and SO4^2−
choices.why: These differ by two protons. A conjugate pair differs by exactly one: H2SO4 and HSO4^−.

choices.text: H3O^+ and OH^−
choices.why: These differ by two protons. H3O^+ pairs with H2O, and OH^− pairs with H2O.

choices.text: HCl and NaCl
choices.why: These differ by swapping H for Na, not by one proton.

explanation: HCO3^− and CO3^2− differ by exactly one proton: HCO3^− is the conjugate acid, and CO3^2− is the conjugate base.

prompt: A student says H3O^+ and OH^− are a conjugate acid-base pair, because one is an acid and the other is a base. What is wrong?

choices.text: Their formulas differ by two protons; each pairs with H2O instead (H3O^+/H2O and H2O/OH^−).
H3O^+ is a base and OH^− is an acid.
choices.why: H3O^+ can donate a proton (acid) and OH^− can accept one (base); the issue is that they differ by two protons.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong.
choices.why: A conjugate pair must differ by exactly one proton. H3O^+ and OH^− differ by two.

choices.text: Only neutral molecules can form conjugate pairs.
choices.why: Ions form conjugate pairs all the time, like NH4^+ and NH3.

explanation: Conjugate pairs differ by one proton. H3O^+ is the conjugate acid of H2O, and OH^− is the conjugate base of H2O, but H3O^+ and OH^− are two protons apart.

prompt: Identify the conjugate acid-base pairs in HC2H3O2 + H2O ⇌ H3O^+ + C2H3O2^−.

choices.text: HC2H3O2/C2H3O2^− and H3O^+/H2O
HC2H3O2/H2O and H3O^+/C2H3O2^−
choices.why: Each pair must differ by one proton. HC2H3O2 and H2O are different substances, not two forms of one.

choices.text: HC2H3O2/H3O^+ and H2O/C2H3O2^−
choices.why: HC2H3O2 and H3O^+ are both acids from different pairs. Match each species with the one it becomes.

choices.text: There is only one pair, HC2H3O2/C2H3O2^−
choices.why: Every Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reaction has two conjugate pairs; water and hydronium are the second.

explanation: HC2H3O2 donates a proton to become C2H3O2^− (one pair), and H2O accepts it to become H3O^+ (the other pair). Every Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reaction can be labeled with two conjugate pairs.

prompt: How many conjugate acid-base pairs can be labeled in every Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reaction?
explanation: Every Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reaction can be labeled with two conjugate acid-base pairs: the acid with its conjugate base, and the base with its conjugate acid.

prompt: The hydrogen sulfate ion, HSO4^−, donates a proton. What is the charge on its conjugate base? (Give it as a signed number, such as −1.)
explanation: Removing a proton (H^+) removes one positive charge: HSO4^− → SO4^2− + H^+. The conjugate base, SO4^2−, has a charge of −2.

prompt: A swimming pool owner cleans the pool with muriatic acid. What is muriatic acid?

choices.text: HCl(aq)
HC2H3O2(aq)
choices.why: A dilute solution of acetic acid is vinegar.

choices.text: NaOH(aq)
choices.why: NaOH is lye, a base.

choices.text: NH3(aq)
choices.why: NH3 is a base found in many cleaning products.

explanation: Muriatic acid is another name for HCl(aq), hydrochloric acid.

prompt: Lye-based drain cleaners are dangerous household chemicals. What is lye?

choices.text: A common name for NaOH (also used for KOH), an extremely caustic base
A common name for HCl, a strong acid
choices.why: HCl(aq) is muriatic acid. Lye is NaOH, a base.

choices.text: A peroxide compound
choices.why: Peroxides are used in safer, non-lye drain cleaners.

choices.text: A name for ammonia
choices.why: Ammonia, NH3, is a milder base in cleaning products. Lye is NaOH.

explanation: Lye is a common name for NaOH, also used for KOH. It is an extremely caustic chemical that attacks clogs, and also body tissues, so it must be handled with great care.

prompt: One explanation for why soap solutions feel slippery is that soaps are slightly basic. How do they make the solution basic?

choices.text: They contain compounds that accept protons from H2O, forming excess OH^− ions.
They contain compounds that donate protons to H2O, forming excess H3O^+ ions.
choices.why: Donating protons would make the solution acidic. Soaps accept protons, leaving extra OH^−.

choices.text: They contain NaOH, which they release as a gas.
choices.why: Soaps act as Brønsted-Lowry bases: they take protons from water, forming OH^−.

choices.text: They remove all the water from the solution.
choices.why: Soaps work in water. They accept protons from it, forming excess OH^−.

explanation: Many soaps are slightly basic because they contain compounds that act as Brønsted-Lowry bases, accepting protons from H2O and forming excess OH^− ions.
